CONTEMPORARY IR — THE STRUCTURAL LANDSCAPE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  THE TRANSITION QUESTION:
  Is the post-Cold War unipolar order ending?
  If so, what comes next?

  THREE ANALYTICAL POSITIONS:
  ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
  │  LIBERAL ORDER   │  GREAT POWER      │  POLYCRISIS /       │
  │  CONTINUITY      │  COMPETITION      │  DISORDER           │
  │                  │                   │                     │
  │  Mearsheimer     │  Mearsheimer      │  Tooze, Runciman    │
  │  wrong; liberals │  right; US-China  │  The world faces    │
  │  right; democra- │  structural       │  compounding crises │
  │  cies adapting   │  conflict coming  │  with no adequate   │
  │                  │                   │  governance         │
  │  Biden's "US is  │  Allison's        │                     │
  │  back" thesis    │  Thucydides Trap  │  Climate + pandemic │
  │                  │                   │  + AI + democratic  │
  │  Institutions    │  Tech decoupling, │  backsliding + geop │
  │  survive; norms  │  mil. buildup,    │  olitical conflict  │
  │  persist         │  Taiwan risk      │  = systemic stress  │
  └──────────────────┴───────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

  STRUCTURAL FORCES SHAPING CONTEMPORARY IR:
  1. US-China strategic competition (technology, military, economy)
  2. Russia's revisionist challenge to European security order
  3. Middle power activism — hedging, coalitions, autonomy
  4. Global South agency — debt, development, multipolarity
  5. Climate change — physical risk + geopolitical disruption
  6. AI and military technology — offense/defense, epistemic security

US-CHINA COMPETITION — STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  MEARSHEIMER'S PREDICTION (offensive realism):
  China's continued rise = China seeking regional hegemony in Asia
  US will resist (just as it resists any hegemon in the Western Hemisphere)
  Result: intense US-China security competition
  "The tragedy of great power politics" — not preference but structure

  WHY STRUCTURAL COMPETITION IS HARD TO AVOID:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SECURITY DILEMMA:                                         │
  │  China's military buildup = defensive from Beijing's view  │
  │  (Taiwan, South China Sea, first island chain)             │
  │  = offensive from US/regional perspective                  │
  │  → Actions each takes for security threaten the other      │
  │  → Spiral of mutual buildup and counter-buildup            │
  │                                                            │
  │  POWER SHIFT TIMELINE:                                     │
  │  GDP at PPP: China already surpassed US (~2017 IMF est.)   │
  │  Military spending: US ~$900B; China ~$300B (official)     │
  │  But China's advantage in its home region is asymmetric    │
  │  A2/AD (anti-access/area denial) means US can't easily     │
  │  project power into western Pacific near China's coast     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  COUNTER: INTERDEPENDENCE CONSTRAINT
  Pre-tariff war trade: ~$700 billion/year
  US debt held by China: ~$1 trillion
  Supply chain interdependence: pharmaceuticals, rare earths,
  electronics components
  Liberal argument: costs of conflict too high for rational actors
  Realist response: this mirrors UK-Germany in 1913 (didn't prevent WWI)

US-CHINA TECH COMPETITION
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  SEMICONDUCTORS (the chokepoint):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CHIP SUPPLY CHAIN (simplified):                          │
  │                                                          │
  │ Design:    ARM (UK), Qualcomm (US), Apple (US)           │
  │            Intel (US), AMD (US)                          │
  │            Huawei/HiSilicon (China, partially blocked)   │
  │                                                          │
  │ EDA Tools: Synopsys/Cadence/Mentor (US) — CHOKEPOINT     │
  │            China cannot design advanced chips without    │
  │            US EDA software                               │
  │                                                          │
  │ Fabrication: TSMC (Taiwan) — most critical node          │
  │              Samsung (South Korea)                       │
  │              Intel (US, rebuilding)                      │
  │              SMIC (China) — 7nm, partially blocked       │
  │                                                          │
  │ Equipment: ASML (Netherlands, EUV — monopoly)            │
  │            Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA (US)     │
  │            Tokyo Electron (Japan)                        │
  │                                                          │
  │ US CONTROLS (2022-2024):                                 │
  │ • Advanced node chip export controls (below 14nm)        │
  │ • EDA software export controls                           │
  │ • NVIDA H100/A100 GPU restrictions                       │
  │ • CHIPS Act: $52B to subsidize US domestic fabs          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AI COMPETITION:
  US advantages: frontier model capability (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic),
  NVIDA GPU dominance (before restrictions), research talent, capital
  China's position: DeepSeek (January 2025) demonstrated parity at
  lower compute cost; large domestic market for AI deployment;
  state coordination advantage for sensitive data access
  Structural question: can AI development be decoupled given
  fundamental research is published globally?

  5G / TELECOM:
  Huawei 5G vs. Ericsson/Nokia/Qualcomm
  US campaign to exclude Huawei from Western telecom infrastructure
  UK, Australia reversed initial Huawei approvals
  Germany: partial exclusion (core network)
  Developing world: Huawei often cheaper — significant deployment
  Standards bodies: ITU, 3GPP — arena for US-China contest
  (connects to internet governance discussion in 07-GLOBAL-GOVERNANCE)

SOUTH CHINA SEA — LEGAL AND MILITARY DIMENSIONS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  NINE-DASH LINE:
  China claims ~90% of South China Sea within "nine-dash line."
  Basis: historical claims; no clear legal foundation under UNCLOS.
  UNCLOS (which China has ratified): EEZ = 200 nautical miles
  from coast. Most of South China Sea exceeds this from any coast.

  PHILIPPINES vs. CHINA (2016):
  International arbitration under UNCLOS Annex VII.
  Tribunal: China's nine-dash line has no legal basis under UNCLOS.
  China rejected tribunal's jurisdiction and ignored ruling.
  US, EU, Japan welcomed ruling; China called it "null and void."
  → Illustrates enforcement gap in international law

  ISLAND-BUILDING CAMPAIGN:
  2014-2016: China dredged and built artificial islands on
  submerged reefs (Spratly Islands) — created ~3,200 acres of land.
  Installed: military airstrips, hangars, radar, missile systems.
  Under UNCLOS: artificial islands on submerged features cannot
  generate territorial waters or EEZ.
  Fait accompli: islands are now built; military capability installed.

  FREEDOM OF NAVIGATION OPERATIONS (FONOPs):
  US Navy regularly transits through South China Sea near
  China's claimed territorial waters.
  Purpose: refuse to recognize Chinese territorial claims through
  non-recognition and practice.
  China protests each FONOP; no military confrontation to date.

  ASEAN DIVISION:
  Philippines, Vietnam oppose Chinese claims most directly.
  Cambodia, Laos effectively Chinese proxies in ASEAN.
  → ASEAN cannot produce unified position.
  → Bilateral deals between China and individual ASEAN members.

blocks.text:
RUSSIA'S WAR IN UKRAINE — ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORKS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  PROXIMATE vs. STRUCTURAL CAUSES:

  RUSSIAN NARRATIVE (Putin's):
  • NATO expansion threatened Russian security (realist frame)
  • Ukraine is not a real nation; historically Russian
  • Western-backed "coup" in 2014 destabilized legitimate government
  • "Denazification and demilitarization" as pretext

  WESTERN/UKRAINIAN ANALYSIS:
  • 2014: Russia annexed Crimea; Minsk Agreements failed to end Donbas conflict
  • 2022 invasion: clear violation of UN Charter Article 2(4)
    (prohibition on threat or use of force against territorial integrity)
  • Putin's maximalist goal: prevent Ukraine from becoming viable
    Western democracy on Russia's border → threat to regime legitimacy

  REALIST DEBATE:
  Mearsheimer (2014+): NATO expansion caused Russian reaction;
  US should have made Ukraine neutral (Finlandization).
  Realist critics: this gives veto over others' sovereignty to
  great powers; Ukraine has right to choose alliances; Russian
  imperialism is not "security" concern but expansionism.

  THE HYBRID WARFARE FRAME:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ "HYBRID WARFARE" — Elements observed in Ukraine 2014-22: │
  │ • Conventional military force                            │
  │ • "Little green men" (ambiguous forces without markings) │
  │ • Cyber attacks (NotPetya 2017, power grid attacks)      │
  │ • Disinformation campaigns (domestic and foreign)        │
  │ • Economic coercion (gas supply manipulation)            │
  │ • Political subversion (electoral interference)          │
  │ • Information operations (RT/Sputnik)                    │
  │                                                          │
  │ Caveat: "hybrid warfare" is partly an analytical         │
  │ construct imposed by Western analysts. Russia sees       │
  │ these as integrated operations, not new doctrine.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MIDDLE POWERS — HEDGING AND STRATEGIC AUTONOMY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  DEFINING MIDDLE POWERS:
  Not superpowers but capable of significant regional/global role.
  Contemporary: India, Brazil, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, South Korea,
  Australia, Indonesia, South Africa, UAE.

  HEDGING BEHAVIOR:
  Middle powers refuse to choose between US and China (or US and Russia).
  Strategic reasoning:
  • Keep options open
  • Extract concessions from both sides
  • Preserve autonomy
  • May genuinely have interests that don't align with either bloc

  INDIA:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ INDIA'S STRATEGIC POSITION:                              │
  │ • Founding member of Non-Aligned Movement                │
  │ • "Strategic autonomy" as consistent doctrine            │
  │ • Buys Russian oil at discount post-2022 sanctions       │
  │ • Abstained on UN GA resolutions condemning Russia       │
  │ • Simultaneously: Quad member (US, Japan, Australia,     │
  │   India — implicit anti-China security grouping)         │
  │ • AUKUS: India not included; watched with interest       │
  │ • India-China border conflict (Galwan Valley 2020)       │
  │   → genuine security concern about China                 │
  │ Result: hedging both sides; benefiting from strategic    │
  │ importance to both.                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TURKEY:
  NATO member; bought Russian S-400 missile system.
  Blocked Swedish/Finnish NATO membership for ~14 months.
  Mediated Ukraine-Russia grain deal (Istanbul, 2022).
  Erdoğan: uses Turkey's position to extract concessions
  from both US/NATO and Russia simultaneously.
  Risks: NATO cohesion; US weapon sales restrictions.

  SAUDI ARABIA / GULF STATES:
  US security guarantees since 1945 (oil for security).
  Post-2022: Saudi joined BRICS; pursuing China ties.
  China brokered Saudi-Iran normalization (2023) — notable
  because China, not US, conducted the diplomacy.
  MBS: deliberately cultivating multiple great power relationships.

  BRAZIL:
  Under Lula (2023+): returned to multilateral engagement.
  "G20 presidency (2024): bridge between Global South/West.
  Ukraine: refused arms to Ukraine; offered mediation.
  Participates in BRICS; maintains US economic ties.

  MIDDLE POWER IMPLICATIONS FOR IR THEORY:
  Neither US-led unipolarity nor US-China bipolarity;
  multipolar world with agency dispersed among mid-sized states.
  This complicates: NATO-style collective security,
  economic sanctions (need broad participation),
  climate agreements (need BASIC — Brazil/South Africa/India/China).

blocks.heading_context: ## The Global South in Contemporary IR
blocks.text:
GLOBAL SOUTH — CONTESTED CONCEPT AND REAL POLITICS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  WHAT IS THE "GLOBAL SOUTH"?
  Not a geographic concept (Australia is in Southern Hemisphere;
  not part of "Global South" analytically).
  = Historically colonized, economically developing states;
  predominantly in Africa, Latin America, South/Southeast Asia.
  Contested because: enormous internal diversity; Brazil/Nigeria/
  Bangladesh have very different interests.
  Political use: solidarity frame against Western dominance in
  international institutions and norms.

  DEBT AND DEVELOPMENT FINANCE:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ BELT AND ROAD INITIATIVE (BRI) — DEBT TRAP DEBATE:       │
  │                                                          │
  │ DEBT TRAP THESIS (Brahma Chellaney, 2017):               │
  │ China extends loans for infrastructure;                  │
  │ countries cannot repay → China gains strategic assets.   │
  │ Hambantota Port (Sri Lanka): leased to China for 99 yrs  │
  │ cited as paradigm case.                                  │
  │                                                          │
  │ COUNTER-EVIDENCE (AidData, Johns Hopkins, others):       │
  │ • Hambantota: Sri Lanka's debt crisis was from           │
  │   international bond markets, not primarily China.       │
  │ • Most BRI loans are commercial, not strategic.          │
  │ • China has renegotiated more than seized assets.        │
  │ • Many BRI projects are overpriced and poor quality.     │
  │   The problem is economic waste, not strategic trap.     │
  │                                                          │
  │ NUANCED ASSESSMENT:                                      │
  │ BRI is significant infrastructure finance where World    │
  │ Bank and Western donors weren't competing.               │
  │ Creates dependence and political influence, not seizure  │
  │ of assets — a subtler form of structural power.          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  G20 REFORM:
  African Union added 2023 (54 countries, 1 seat).
  Demand: reform IMF/World Bank voting shares to reflect
  current economic size (China, India underrepresented
  vs. their global GDP share).
  Loss and damage fund (climate): COP27 (2022) created fund
  for developing countries' climate losses — paid by
  developed countries.

  BRICS EXPANSION (2023):
  Invited: Saudi Arabia, Iran, UAE, Ethiopia, Egypt, Argentina
  (Argentina later declined under Milei).
  BRICS+ now covers: ~46% of world population, ~37% of global GDP (PPP)
  But: no shared institutions, currency, or strategic alignment.
  India and China are BRICS members AND have border conflicts.
  Brazil under Lula vs. Russia's expansionism: fundamentally different.
  BRICS is a political platform, not a coherent bloc.
  (Revisits the confusion point from 07-GLOBAL-GOVERNANCE)

  POSTCOLONIAL CRITIQUES IN PRACTICE:
  Developing states in UN forums consistently challenge:
  • IP protection for pharmaceuticals (COVID vaccine access)
  • Agricultural subsidies in developed countries (WTO Doha failure)
  • Climate "common but differentiated responsibilities"
    (historical emissions justify developing country carve-outs)
  • R2P as regime change cover (Libya outcome)
  These aren't just theory — they are positions at actual negotiations.

blocks.heading_context: ## Climate Change as an IR Challenge
blocks.text:
CLIMATE CHANGE — GEOPOLITICAL DIMENSIONS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  PHYSICAL RISK → GEOPOLITICAL RISK PATHWAY:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ SEA LEVEL RISE:                                          │
  │ Maldives, Bangladesh, Pacific Islands → displacement     │
  │ Bangladesh: 20-30 million potentially displaced by 2050  │
  │ → Regional migration pressures (India, Myanmar)          │
  │                                                          │
  │ WATER SCARCITY:                                          │
  │ Nile (Egypt-Ethiopia-Sudan): Grand Ethiopian Renaissance │
  │ Dam; Egypt views reduced Nile flow as existential threat │
  │ Indus (India-Pakistan): treaty under strain              │
  │ Mekong (China-Southeast Asia): China dams upstream       │
  │ Water conflicts: classified as "threat multiplier" by    │
  │ US DoD.                                                  │
  │                                                          │
  │ FOOD SECURITY:                                           │
  │ Ukraine-Russia: 30% of world wheat exports at risk       │
  │ Climate-driven crop failures → food price shocks         │
  │ → Political instability (Arab Spring 2011 preceded       │
  │   by 2010 wheat price spike)                             │
  │                                                          │
  │ MIGRATION:                                               │
  │ Heat zones: parts of Middle East, South Asia, Sahel      │
  │ may become unlivable during summer by 2050 (wet-bulb     │
  │ temperature limit for human outdoor survival)            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  GREEN INDUSTRIAL POLICY COMPETITION:
  IRA (US Inflation Reduction Act, 2022): $370B in clean energy
  subsidies → attracts EV, solar, battery manufacturing to US.
  EU response: "Net Zero Industry Act" — not wanting to lose
  manufacturing to US subsidies. Trade friction with EU allies.
  China: dominant in solar panels (~80% of global production),
  EV batteries (CATL, BYD), rare earth processing.

  RARE EARTH COMPETITION:
  17 rare earth elements critical for clean energy transition:
  neodymium (wind turbines/EVs), lithium (batteries),
  cobalt (batteries — DRC), dysprosium (EV motors).
  China: ~60% of rare earth mining; ~85% of processing.
  US, Australia, Canada: diversification efforts.
  → Clean energy transition depends on supply chains that
    currently run through geopolitical competitor.

  CLIMATE AND GREAT POWER COMPETITION:
  Paradox: US-China competition makes climate cooperation harder,
  but both need climate cooperation.
  Kerry-Xie climate track: maintained even during tech/security tensions.
  "Climate club" concept (Nordhaus): group of states imposing
  carbon tariffs on non-members → trade measure to enforce
  climate compliance. EU CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism)
  is early version of this. China opposes.

AI IN IR — MILITARY, INTELLIGENCE, AND EPISTEMIC SECURITY
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  MILITARY AI:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS SYSTEMS (AWS):                        │
  │                                                          │
  │ Current: semi-autonomous (human-on-the-loop or in-loop)  │
  │ CIWS (Close-In Weapon System): automated anti-missile    │
  │ Iron Dome: automated intercept decisions                 │
  │ Loitering munitions (Switchblade, Harop): human launch;  │
  │   autonomous terminal guidance                           │
  │                                                          │
  │ DEBATE:                                                  │
  │ FOR lethal autonomous weapons:                           │
  │ • Faster decision loop (sub-second; human can't keep up) │
  │ • Remove humans from harm                                │
  │ • More precise (no anger, no fear, no panic)             │
  │                                                          │
  │ AGAINST (Campaign to Stop Killer Robots):                │
  │ • Accountability gap (who is responsible for a war crime │
  │   by an autonomous weapon?)                              │
  │ • Lowering threshold for conflict (no human casualties   │
  │   on deploying side = no political cost)                 │
  │ • AI errors in novel environments (adversarial attacks,  │
  │   unexpected scenarios)                                  │
  │ • Escalation risk (machine-speed warfare)                │
  │                                                          │
  │ STATUS: No binding international treaty; UN discussions  │
  │ ongoing since 2013 (Convention on Certain                │
  │ Conventional Weapons framework). US, Russia, China       │
  │ all developing autonomous capabilities.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AI IN INTELLIGENCE:
  ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance) transformed by:
  • AI-enabled satellite imagery analysis (Planet Labs + ML)
  • OSINT (open-source intelligence) — social media, commercial imagery
    → This is what revealed Russian military buildup before Feb 2022
    → US/UK declassified intelligence to deny Russia narrative control
  • Facial recognition at border/checkpoint (surveillance technology exports)
  • Signal intelligence automated triage

  EPISTEMIC SECURITY:
  Deepfakes and disinformation at scale:
  • 2024 election cycle: AI-generated political ads, synthetic media
  • Slovak election 2023: deepfake audio of candidate circulated
    45 minutes before voting silence period
  • Context collapse: false information spreads before correction

  State-sponsored information operations:
  Russia (Internet Research Agency), China (Spamouflage/Dragonbridge),
  Iran: ongoing campaigns to influence Western public opinion.
  Scale enabled by: automated account generation, LLM-generated text,
  targeted ad placement on social platforms.

  Response mechanisms:
  • Platform labeling (Meta, Google, X/Twitter — inconsistent)
  • Government warnings (pre-election briefings)
  • Media literacy programs
  • Technical detection (C2PA — content provenance standard)
  None are sufficient at current scale.

  AI GOVERNANCE IN IR:
  No binding international AI treaty yet.
  Bletchley AI Safety Summit (2023): 28 states + EU signed
  "Bletchley Declaration" — general principles, no binding commitments.
  US AI Safety Institute; UK AI Safety Institute; EU AI Act
  (risk-based regulation, enforceable within EU).
  China: domestic AI regulations (generative AI content rules 2023).
  US-China: no bilateral AI governance dialogue as of 2024.
  GPAI (Global Partnership on AI): 29 members; aspirational.
  Standards track: ISO/IEC JTC 1 SC 42 — AI standards
  (the arena where MSFT and tech sector compete with Chinese standards bodies)

POLYCRISIS — COMPOUNDING SYSTEMIC RISKS
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ORIGIN:
  Edgar Morin (1970s French sociologist): complex systems
  Adam Tooze (historian) popularized: "polycrisis" as
  simultaneous, interacting crises that compound each other
  in ways that exceed the sum of their parts.

  WHY "POLYCRISIS" IS ANALYTICALLY USEFUL:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TRADITIONAL IR FRAMEWORK: handle crises one at a time    │
  │ • Great power competition (one analysis)                 │
  │ • Climate change (another analysis)                      │
  │ • Pandemic governance (another)                          │
  │ • Democratic backsliding (another)                       │
  │                                                          │
  │ POLYCRISIS INSIGHT: these interact                       │
  │ • COVID → supply chain disruption → inflation →          │
  │   political populism → democratic backsliding            │
  │ • Climate → food insecurity → migration →                │
  │   right-wing politics → Paris Agreement defection        │
  │ • Ukraine war → energy crisis → industrial recession →   │
  │   reduced climate investment                             │
  │ • AI disruption → labor dislocation → political anger    │
  │   → protectionism → deglobalization                      │
  │                                                          │
  │ The system isn't just stressed; it's in compounding      │
  │ stress where each shock weakens the capacity to          │
  │ respond to the next.                                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  GOVERNANCE FAILURES THAT AMPLIFY POLYCRISIS:
  • UNSC paralysis: can't address major security crises
  • WTO Appellate Body collapse: trade disputes unresolvable
  • WHO authority limits: pandemic response without enforcement
  • Paris NDC gap: climate targets not met
  • G20 Ukraine deadlock: economic governance body paralyzed on security
  Each institution's weakness leaves a gap the others can't fill.

  THE "RESILIENCE" RESPONSE:
  Policy pivot from optimization to resilience:
  • Supply chain reshoring / "friend-shoring" (CHIPS Act, IRA)
  • Strategic stockpiles (PPE, energy, food)
  • Redundancy over efficiency
  • Diversification of critical dependencies
  This is a retreat from 1990s globalization logic:
  comparative advantage → resilience-first

  THE DEGLOBALIZATION QUESTION:
  Trade share of GDP: peaked ~2008; declined somewhat;
  still very high historically.
  Is deglobalization happening? Ambiguous:
  • Goods trade: some reshoring, but total volumes remain high
  • Technology: significant decoupling in advanced chips/AI
  • Finance: capital still largely globalized
  • Data: major localization pressures (GDPR, India, China)
  More accurate: "slowbalization" or selective decoupling
  (high-tech and security-sensitive areas) rather than
  full deglobalization.
